children.title: Failure of Proto-Differentiability
children.top_down_role: Breakdown of graphical derivative limits for subgradient or normal mappings.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) has locally closed graph at \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{Liminf}_{t\downarrow0}Q_t\ne\operatorname*{Limsup}_{t\downarrow0}Q_t\).

notation.meaning: graphical difference quotient of the graph

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: proto-differentiability is defined by graphical convergence of difference quotients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graphical proto-differentiability for a finite-dimensional set-valued mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(t>0\), set
\[
Q_t:=\left\{(u,v):\bigl(\bar x+tu,\bar y+tv\bigr)\in\operatorname{gph}F\right\}.
\]
The mapping \(F\) fails to be proto-differentiable at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) when the sets \(Q_t\) do not converge in the Painlevé–Kuratowski sense as \(t\downarrow0\); equivalently,
\[
\operatorname*{Liminf}_{t\downarrow0}Q_t
\ne
\operatorname*{Limsup}_{t\downarrow0}Q_t.
\]
The outer limit alone still defines the graph of the graphical derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proto-differentiability fails when the rescaled graphs have unequal inner and outer set limits, even though the outer limit still yields a graphical derivative.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Proto-Differentiability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The graphical-limit formulation is plausible and internally consistent, but no citation is supplied to verify the precise proto-differentiability convention or the assertion that the outer limit is the graphical derivative.

children.title: Failure of Parabolic Derivability
children.top_down_role: Mismatch between attainable second-order arcs and outer tangent models.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\in C\).
\(w\in T_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_C^{2,i}(\bar x,w)\ne T_C^{2,o}(\bar x,w)\).

notation.meaning: inner and outer second-order tangent sets

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: parabolic derivability is equality of inner and outer second-order tangent limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential finite-dimensional definition using second-order feasible arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
S_t:=\left\{z:\bar x+tw+\tfrac12t^2z\in C\right\},\qquad
T_C^{2,i}(\bar x,w):=\operatorname*{Liminf}_{t\downarrow0}S_t,
\quad
T_C^{2,o}(\bar x,w):=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{t\downarrow0}S_t.
\]
Parabolic derivability of \(C\) at \(\bar x\) in direction \(w\) fails when
\[
T_C^{2,i}(\bar x,w)\ne T_C^{2,o}(\bar x,w).
\]
Thus some outer second-order tangent vector is attainable only along selected vanishing scales, rather than along every sufficiently small scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parabolic derivability fails when an outer second-order tangent vector cannot be realized along every vanishing scale by feasible second-order arcs.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Parabolic Derivability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inner-versus-outer second-order tangent formulation is plausible, but an authoritative locator is required to confirm the scaling convention and exact equivalence used for parabolic derivability.

children.title: Loss of Prox-Regularity
children.top_down_role: Unstable proximal geometry and loss of standard second-order correspondences.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\((\bar x,\bar v)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\) and \(f(\bar x)\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No local uniform quadratic lower support exists around \((\bar x,\bar v)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: prox-regularity is characterized by a uniform local quadratic support inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of prox-regularity at a specified function–subgradient pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Prox-regularity of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) is lost when, for every \(r\ge0\) and every neighborhood \(U\) of \((\bar x,\bar v)\), there exist \((x,v)\in U\cap\operatorname{gph}\partial f\) and \(x'\) arbitrarily near \(\bar x\), with \(f(x)\) near \(f(\bar x)\), such that
\[
f(x')<f(x)+\langle v,x'-x\rangle-\frac r2\|x'-x\|^2.
\]
Hence no uniform local quadratic lower support controls nearby subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prox-regularity is lost when every proposed local quadratic support modulus is violated by nearby points and nearby subgradients.
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Prox-Regularity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The intended failure boundary is appropriate, but phrases such as “arbitrarily near” and “f(x) near” do not give the exact quantified negation of prox-regularity. A source is needed to fix the neighborhood, value-truncation, and modulus quantifiers reliably.

children.title: Second-Order Calculus Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Qualification, exactness, and compactness boundaries in second-order calculus.

children.title: Second-Order Qualification Failure
children.top_down_role: Breakdown of exact sum, chain, preimage, or inverse calculus.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
\(G:\mathbb R^m\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^p\) has locally closed graph at \((F(\bar x),\bar z)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^*G(F(\bar x),\bar z)(0)\cap\ker\nabla F(\bar x)^*\ne\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: limiting coderivative of the outer mapping
adjoint Jacobian of the inner mapping

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coderivative qualification failure for a smooth-inner set-valued composition.

source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the composition \(H:=G\circ F\), the basic coderivative qualification at \((\bar x,\bar z)\) fails when
\[
D^*G\bigl(F(\bar x),\bar z\bigr)(0)
\cap
\ker\nabla F(\bar x)^*
\ne\{0\}.
\]
A nonzero element in this intersection is an abnormal multiplier annihilated by the inner Jacobian. Under this failure, second-order chain formulas derived from multiplier elimination are not guaranteed to be exact and may yield only inclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The composition qualification fails when a nonzero abnormal outer multiplier is annihilated by the inner Jacobian, preventing guaranteed exact second-order chain calculus.
knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Qualification Failure

children.title: Exactness Gaps in Second-Order Calculus
children.top_down_role: Separation between upper estimates, lower estimates, and exact second-order representations.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal Q\) is a second-order object at fixed base data.
\(\mathcal L\) and \(\mathcal U\) are valid lower and upper calculus estimates for the same data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal L\subseteq\mathcal Q\subseteq\mathcal U\) with at least one strict inclusion.
review_flags: abstract formulation covering sum, chain, and preimage rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract exactness boundary for set-valued second-order calculus rules.

source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal Q\) denote the target second-order set produced by an exact sum, chain, or preimage rule, and let \(\mathcal L\) and \(\mathcal U\) be established estimates satisfying
\[
\mathcal L\subseteq\mathcal Q\subseteq\mathcal U.
\]
An exactness gap occurs when
\[
\mathcal L\ne\mathcal Q\quad\text{or}\quad\mathcal Q\ne\mathcal U.
\]
Equality of the estimates, \(\mathcal L=\mathcal U\), is sufficient for exactness; validity of only one inclusion is not an exact representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A second-order exactness gap exists when a valid lower or upper calculus estimate differs strictly from the target second-order object.
knowledge_statements.title: Exactness Gaps in Second-Order Calculus

children.title: Dimension-Dependent Calculus Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Dependence of limiting and coderivative calculus on compactness and Asplund-space structure.

children.title: Finite-Dimensional Calculus Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Calculus boundaries specific to finite-dimensional variational settings.

assumptions_latex: \((z_k)\) is bounded in \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(k_j\uparrow\infty\) and \(z\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \(z_{k_j}\to z\).

notation.meaning: bounded sequence of normalized directions or multipliers

review_flags: calculus consequence stated through finite-dimensional compactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional sequential compactness underlying limiting calculus arguments.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Extremal Principle in Variational Analysis p. 171
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Every bounded sequence \((z_k)\subset\mathbb R^n\) admits a strongly convergent subsequence:
\[
\exists\,k_j\uparrow\infty,\ \exists\,z\in\mathbb R^n
\quad\text{such that}\quad z_{k_j}\to z.
\]
Consequently, a finite-dimensional second-order calculus argument that produces bounded normalized directions or multipliers may pass to a strong cluster point without an additional compactness assumption. This mechanism does not itself replace constraint qualifications or closedness conditions required by the calculus rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, bounded multiplier or direction sequences have strongly convergent subsequences, removing one compactness obstacle but not qualification or closedness requirements.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Calculus Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 2. Extremal Principle in Variational Analysis p. 171

children.title: Infinite-Dimensional Calculus Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Calculus boundaries arising in infinite-dimensional variational settings.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\ell^2\) with canonical unit vectors \((e_k)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((e_k)\) is bounded but has no norm-convergent subsequence.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical orthonormal sequences witness failure of norm compactness in infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete obstruction to strong subsequence extraction in infinite-dimensional calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In \(X=\ell^2\), let \(e_k\) be the canonical unit vectors. Then \(\|e_k\|=1\) for every \(k\), while for \(j\ne k\),
\[
\|e_j-e_k\|=\sqrt2.
\]
Hence \((e_k)\) is bounded but has no norm-Cauchy, and therefore no norm-convergent, subsequence. Thus boundedness alone cannot justify strong limiting directions or multipliers in infinite-dimensional second-order calculus; additional compactness, weak-topology, or structural hypotheses are necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The canonical unit vectors in ℓ² form a bounded sequence with no norm-convergent subsequence, invalidating finite-dimensional compactness arguments in strong topology.
knowledge_statements.title: Infinite-Dimensional Calculus Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ℓ² orthonormal-sequence counterexample is mathematically correct and fits the infinite-dimensional boundary leaf, but the record supplies no inspectable source locator.

children.title: Compactness-Dependent Exactness
children.top_down_role: Dependence of limiting second-order calculus on compactness-type properties.

assumptions_latex: \(K\) is compact in a metric space.
\(z_k\in K\) and \(R(z_k)\to0\).
The residual map \(R\) has closed zero-level passage along convergent sequences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Some cluster point \(\bar z\in K\) satisfies \(R(\bar z)=0\).

notation.meaning: compact set containing approximate second-order certificates
residual defining the exact calculus relation

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: compactness plus sequential closedness converts approximate relations into exact limiting relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract compactness mechanism behind exact limiting second-order formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose approximate multipliers or directions \((z_k)\) lie in a compact set \(K\), and their calculus residuals satisfy \(R(z_k)\to0\). If convergence \(z_{k_j}\to z\) together with \(R(z_{k_j})\to0\) implies \(R(z)=0\), then compactness yields a subsequence and a point \(\bar z\in K\) such that
\[
z_{k_j}\to\bar z
\quad\text{and}\quad
R(\bar z)=0.
\]
Thus the approximate second-order relation becomes exact. Without relative compactness, boundedness alone need not provide such a strong cluster point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compactness and sequential closedness turn approximate multiplier or direction relations into an exact limiting relation; boundedness alone may not suffice.
knowledge_statements.title: Compactness-Dependent Exactness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compactness argument is plausible, but the codomain and convergence structure for R are not specified, and no source or concrete second-order calculus application supports the claimed exactness mechanism.

children.title: Asplund-Space Dependence
children.top_down_role: Dependence of coderivative or limiting constructions on Asplund-space structure.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space.
First- and second-order constructions use Fréchet normals or subgradients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Outside Asplund spaces, the stated dense differentiability guarantee fails, so calculus derived from Fréchet constructions is not universally justified.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for calculus based on Fréchet constructions in general Banach spaces.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Extremal Principle in Variational Analysis p. 171
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Banach space \(X\) is Asplund precisely when every continuous convex function on every open convex subset of \(X\) is Fréchet differentiable on a dense set. Consequently, if \(X\) is not Asplund, this differentiability property fails for some continuous convex function. Thus any second-order sum, chain, or normal-cone rule whose derivation requires dense Fréchet differentiability, sequential Fréchet-normal approximation, or fuzzy Fréchet calculus cannot be asserted for arbitrary functions on \(X\) without additional structure. In particular, formulas constructed through \(\widehat\partial f\) and then passed to \(\partial f\) require an Asplund hypothesis or a separate replacement argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Non-Asplund spaces lack the dense Fréchet differentiability guarantee underlying many limiting-normal and second-order calculus rules.
knowledge_statements.title: Asplund-Space Dependence

children.title: Constraint-Geometry Failure Boundaries

children.title: Multiplier Nonuniqueness
children.top_down_role: Competing multiplier-dependent curvature tests and unstable dual selections.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier Nonuniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A degenerate nonlinear program exhibiting multiplier-dependent curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At \(\bar x=(0,0)\), both constraints are active and stationarity is equivalent to \(\lambda_1=\lambda_2\). Hence \(\Lambda(\bar x)=\{(t,t):t\geq0\}\). For the critical direction \(d=(1,0)\), the Lagrangian satisfies \[\langle d,\nabla_{xx}^2L(\bar x,(t,t))d\rangle=-2t.\] Thus different valid multipliers give different second-order tests, including zero curvature at \(t=0\) and strictly negative curvature for \(t>0\). A curvature condition evaluated at an unspecified multiplier therefore does not define a multiplier-independent property of this primal stationary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonunique multipliers at the same stationary point yield incompatible Lagrangian curvature values in one fixed critical direction.
assumptions_latex: The nonlinear program has constraints \(g_1(x)=x_2-x_1^2\leq0\) and \(g_2(x)=-x_2\leq0\).
The reference point is \(\bar x=(0,0)\), with zero objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The multiplier-dependent Lagrangian curvature in direction \(d=(1,0)\) ranges over \((-infty,0]\), although the primal point and direction are fixed.

notation.meaning: set of KKT multipliers at the reference point

children.title: Critical Multiplier Pathologies
children.top_down_role: Multiplier criticality obstructing stability and fast local numerical behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) and the objective are twice continuously differentiable.
\((\bar x,\bar\lambda)\) satisfies the KKT system for \(g(x)\leq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonzero solution of the homogeneous linearized KKT system makes \(\bar\lambda\) critical and obstructs the usual nonsingularity-based stability conclusions.

notation.meaning: graphical derivative of the normal-cone mapping

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criticality criterion for a smooth inequality-constrained KKT system.

source_refs.locator: 5.2.2 Variational Systems as Equilibrium Constraints p. 51
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The multiplier \( ar\lambda\) is critical if there exist \(\xi
eq0\) and \(\eta\) satisfying \[
abla_{xx}^2L( ar x, ar\lambda)\xi+
abla g( ar x)^*\eta=0,\qquad \eta\in DN_{\mathbb R_-^m}(g( ar x)\mid ar\lambda)(
abla g( ar x)\xi).\] This is a nontrivial kernel condition for the homogeneous linearization of the KKT generalized equation. Consequently, the linearized system is not strongly invertible at \(( ar x, ar\lambda)\); conclusions requiring such invertibility, including isolated calmness of the primal-dual solution map or superlinear behavior of corresponding Newton-type iterations, cannot be inferred.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A critical multiplier creates a nontrivial kernel in the linearized KKT system, defeating nonsingularity-based stability and fast-convergence conclusions.
knowledge_statements.title: Critical Multiplier Pathologies

source_witnesses.locator: 5.2.2 Variational Systems as Equilibrium Constraints p. 51
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

children.title: Constraint Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Loss of regular critical-cone, multiplier, and normal-mapping representations.

assumptions_latex: \(h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is twice continuously differentiable.
\(h(\bar x)=0\), and a KKT multiplier \(\bar\lambda\) exists.
The Jacobian \(\nabla h(\bar x)\) lacks full row rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Multiplier uniqueness and nonsingularity of the primal-dual linearization fail whenever \(\ker\nabla h(\bar x)^*\neq\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-constraint degeneracy expressed through rank loss.

source_refs.locator: 4.3.2 Lipschitzian Stability of Constraint Systems p. 414
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Because \(
abla h( ar x)\) lacks full row rank, there is \(\eta
eq0\) with \(
abla h( ar x)^*\eta=0\). If \( ar\lambda\) satisfies stationarity, then every \( ar\lambda+t\eta\) also satisfies stationarity. Moreover, the linearized KKT matrix \[ egin{pmatrix}
abla_{xx}^2L( ar x, ar\lambda)&
abla h( ar x)^*\ 
abla h( ar x)&0\end{pmatrix}\] maps \((0,\eta)\) to zero. Hence the multiplier is nonisolated and the primal-dual linearization is singular. Representations or stability criteria requiring unique multipliers, LICQ, or an invertible KKT system are therefore unavailable without an alternative regularity condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank-deficient equality gradients produce nonunique multipliers and a singular linearized KKT system.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Degeneracy

children.title: Nonpolyhedral Curvature Effects
children.top_down_role: Curvature contributions absent from polyhedral reductions but essential in conic systems.

assumptions_latex: \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x\|\leq1\}\).
\(\|\bar x\|=1\) and \(\bar v=\lambda\bar x\) with \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(w\perp\bar x\), \(DN_C(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w)=\lambda w+\mathbb R\bar x\), displaying a curvature term absent for a polyhedral halfspace.

notation.meaning: normal-cone mapping of the Euclidean unit ball

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-ball example separating curved and polyhedral normal-cone derivatives.

source_refs.locator: 4.4 Sensitivity Analysis for Variational Systems p. 421
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the Euclidean unit ball, feasible graph perturbations at \((\bar x,\bar v)\) with \(\bar v=\lambda\bar x\) and \(\lambda>0\) require \(\langle\bar x,w\rangle=0\), and direct differentiation of \(v=\mu x\) gives \[DN_C(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w)=\lambda w+\mathbb R\bar x.\] The term \(\lambda w\) is the curvature contribution of the sphere. For the tangent halfspace having the same normal direction at \(\bar x\), the corresponding derivative in tangent directions is only \(\mathbb R\bar x\). Replacing a nonpolyhedral constraint by its first-order polyhedral model therefore loses essential second-order curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unit ball's normal-cone derivative contains a tangential curvature term that its tangent halfspace does not retain.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonpolyhedral Curvature Effects

children.title: Representation-Characterization Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Boundaries separating primal, dual, convexified, growth, and stability information.

children.title: Graphical-Coderivative Duality Failure
children.top_down_role: Failure of primal and dual derivative constructions to determine one another.

children.title: Graphical-Derivative Information Loss
children.top_down_role: Primal derivative information not recoverable from the available dual representation.

assumptions_latex: \(F_0,F_2:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\) are the single-valued maps \(F_0(x)=0\) and \(F_2(x)=x^2\).
Both graphs are considered at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(DF_0(0\mid0)=DF_2(0\mid0)\), their second-order graphical behavior differs.

notation.meaning: graphical derivative of a set-valued mapping

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth scalar graphs with identical tangents but different curvature.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.4 Graphical Regularity of Lipschitzian Mappings p. 327
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Both mappings have the same graphical derivative at the origin: \[DF_0(0\mid0)(w)=DF_2(0\mid0)(w)=\{0\}\quad\text{for every }w\in\mathbb R.\] Nevertheless, along \(x(t)=tw\), the graph of \(F_0\) has zero quadratic displacement, whereas \(F_2(tw)=t^2w^2\). Under the normalization \(F(tw)=F(0)+tDF(0)(w)+\tfrac12t^2z+o(t^2)\), the respective second-order displacements are \(z=0\) and \(z=2w^2\). Hence first-order graphical-derivative data do not determine second-order graph curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maps zero and square have the same graphical derivative at zero but different second-order graph displacement.
knowledge_statements.title: Graphical-Derivative Information Loss

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2.4 Graphical Regularity of Lipschitzian Mappings p. 327
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Coderivative Information Loss
children.top_down_role: Dual derivative information not recoverable from the available primal representation.

assumptions_latex: \(F_0(x)=0\) and \(F_2(x)=x^2\) are viewed as single-valued mappings from \(\mathbb R\) to \(\mathbb R\).
Coderivatives are evaluated at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The identical coderivatives \(D^*F_0(0\mid0)=D^*F_2(0\mid0)\) do not determine their distinct second derivatives.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth scalar maps with identical coderivatives but different second derivatives.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.4 Graphical Regularity of Lipschitzian Mappings p. 327
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a smooth single-valued mapping, the coderivative is the adjoint derivative. Since \(F_0'(0)=F_2'(0)=0\), \[D^*F_0(0\mid0)(y^*)=D^*F_2(0\mid0)(y^*)=\{0\}\quad\text{for every }y^*\in\mathbb R.\] However, \(F_0''(0)=0\) while \(F_2''(0)=2\). Thus the first-order limiting coderivative at one graph point contains no information distinguishing the two second-order curvatures. Additional neighborhood, directional, or second-order coderivative information is required for such a determination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero and square have identical coderivatives at the origin, yet their second derivatives are zero and two.
knowledge_statements.title: Coderivative Information Loss

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2.4 Graphical Regularity of Lipschitzian Mappings p. 327
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Primal–Dual Determination Failure
children.top_down_role: Regimes where primal or dual derivative constructions fail to determine their counterpart.

assumptions_latex: \(C=(\mathbb R\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb R)\subset\mathbb R^2\).
Tangent and limiting-normal cones are taken at the origin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For this nonregular set, \(N_C(0)\neq T_C(0)^\circ\), so tangent data do not determine limiting-normal data by polarity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cross-shaped set showing failure of tangent–limiting-normal polarity.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.4 Graphical Regularity of Lipschitzian Mappings p. 327
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At the origin, the tangent cone is the union of the two coordinate axes: \[T_C(0)=C.\] Its negative polar is \(T_C(0)^\circ=\{0\}\), because a polar vector must annihilate both axes. By approaching the origin through nonzero points of either branch, the limiting normal cone is instead \[N_C(0)=(\mathbb R\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb R)=C.\] Therefore \(N_C(0)\neq T_C(0)^\circ\). Applied to a graph, this shows that the primal graphical derivative does not determine the limiting coderivative through polarity when graphical regularity is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the union of coordinate axes, the tangent polar is zero while the limiting normal cone contains both axes.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Determination Failure

children.title: Mismatch Regularity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regularity distinctions controlling agreement or mismatch between derivative representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Mismatch Regularity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity boundary for tangent–normal primal–dual formulas in finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The graphical derivative is determined by \(T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\), whereas the limiting coderivative is determined by \(N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\). The regular normal always satisfies \[\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)=T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)^\circ.\] To recover the limiting normal from this tangent polar, one additionally needs a regime in which \(N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)=\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\), such as Clarke regularity at the reference point. Without that equality, the limiting normal can contain branch normals absent from the tangent polar, so the limiting coderivative cannot in general be reconstructed solely from the graphical derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tangent polar determines the regular normal, but it need not determine the limiting normal or coderivative when graphical regularity fails.
assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb R^n\), \(Y=\mathbb R^m\), and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has a locally closed graph at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
The graph is not assumed Clarke regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without graphical regularity, \(D^*F\) need not equal the polar-dual construction obtained from \(DF\).

children.title: Convexification Information Loss
children.top_down_role: Loss of branch-specific or directional curvature in convexified generalized Hessians.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(f(x)=x|x|\).
The generalized Hessian is the Clarke generalized Jacobian of \(f'\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convexification changes the branch set \(\{-2,2\}\) into \([-2,2]\), introducing curvature values not realized by either smooth branch.

notation.meaning: limiting Jacobian set of the gradient

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional piecewise-quadratic example of convexification loss.

source_refs.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function is continuously differentiable with \(f'(x)=2|x|\). Its classical second derivatives are \(2\) for \(x>0\) and \(-2\) for \(x<0\), so the limiting branch set is \[\partial_B f'(0)=\{-2,2\}.\] Convexification gives the Clarke generalized Hessian \[\partial_C^2f(0)=\operatorname{co}\{-2,2\}=[-2,2].\] In particular, \(0\) belongs to the convexified object although no adjacent smooth branch has zero curvature. The convexified Hessian therefore cannot identify which branch produced a curvature value and may obscure direction-specific positive or negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexifying the two branch curvatures adds zero and all intermediate values, erasing branch identity and directional sign.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexification Information Loss

children.title: Growth–Curvature Nonequivalence
children.top_down_role: Regimes where second-order positivity, quadratic growth, and strong minimality cease to coincide.

knowledge_statements.title: Growth–Curvature Nonequivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional loss of uniformity between positivity and quadratic growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function is continuous and twice Fréchet differentiable, and for every nonzero \(h\in\ell^2\), \[\langle\nabla^2f(0)h,h\rangle=2\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{h_n^2}{n}>0.\] Thus its Hessian is positive definite in the pointwise sense. Nevertheless, no \(\kappa>0\) and neighborhood of zero satisfy \(f(x)\geq\kappa\|x\|^2\): for every sufficiently small \(t>0\), \[\frac{f(te_n)}{\|te_n\|^2}=\frac1n\longrightarrow0.\] Hence positive definiteness without a uniform modulus is not equivalent to quadratic growth or strong local minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A diagonal quadratic on ell-squared has positive curvature in every nonzero direction but no uniform quadratic-growth modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty x_n^2/n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pointwise positive Hessian curvature does not imply uniform quadratic growth in infinite dimensions.

children.title: Stability-Characterization Failure
children.top_down_role: Loss of tilt- or full-stability equivalences when required regularity is absent.

knowledge_statements.title: Stability-Characterization Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional failure of a positivity-based tilt-stability characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Although \(\nabla^2f(0)\) is positive definite, its eigenvalues \(2/n\) approach zero. The gradient operator \(A\) therefore has no bounded local inverse. Indeed, the formal stationary point of \(f(x)-\langle v,x\rangle\) satisfies \[x_n=\frac n2v_n.\] For arbitrarily small \(v\in\ell^2\), this sequence need not belong to \(\ell^2\); even on the range of \(A\), the inverse is not Lipschitz. Thus the localized argmin mapping is not a single-valued Lipschitz map on a neighborhood of zero, and neither tilt stability nor strong metric regularity follows from nonuniform positive definiteness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vanishing Hessian eigenvalues make the tilt solution map undefined or non-Lipschitz despite positive curvature in every direction.
assumptions_latex: \(X=\ell^2\) and \(f(x)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty x_n^2/n\).
Tilt stability is measured using perturbations \(f(x)-\langle v,x\rangle\) with \(v\in\ell^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive definiteness of \(\nabla^2f(0)\) alone does not imply tilt stability or strong metric regularity of \(\partial f\).

children.title: Numerical Implication Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Boundaries where second-order analytical information does not support the expected local numerical behavior.

children.title: Generalized-Derivative Singularity
children.top_down_role: Failure of local Newton models through singular generalized derivatives.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is locally Lipschitz and semismooth near a zero \(\bar x\).
The Newton step uses \(V_k\in\partial_C F(x_k)\) and solves \(V_k s_k=-F(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\{\det V:V\in\partial_C F(\bar x)\}\) destroys the uniform invertibility needed for the standard local superlinear conclusion.

notation.meaning: Clarke generalized Jacobian of F at x
Newton linearization selected at iteration k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional semismooth Newton boundary expressed through loss of generalized-Jacobian invertibility.

source_refs.locator: 7.1 Nonsmooth Analysis I: Clarke's Calculus p. 626
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II
The Linear Complementarity Problem

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Uniform nonsingularity of all matrices in \(\partial_C F(x)\) for \(x\) near \(\bar x\), together with semismoothness, supports well-defined local Newton steps and superlinear convergence. If \(\partial_C F(\bar x)\) contains a singular matrix, that conclusion cannot be inferred for arbitrary selections. For the scalar mapping \(F(x)=x^2\), one has \(\partial_C F(0)=\{0\}\); the inverse model is unavailable at the solution, while for \(x_k\ne0\) Newton gives \(x_{k+1}=x_k/2\), only linear convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular generalized derivative can make the Newton equation unsolvable or reduce its rate; for F(x)=x², Newton converges only linearly to the singular zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Derivative Singularity

children.title: Model-Fidelity Rate Boundary
children.top_down_role: Loss of fast local convergence through inaccurate derivative models or unstable active geometry.

children.title: Second-Order Model Fidelity
children.top_down_role: Accuracy regimes for generalized second-order models near a reference solution.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), \(f(\bar x)\) is finite, and \(\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x)\).
The second subderivative \(d^2 f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\) is defined on the directions under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model has second-order fidelity precisely when its remainder is \(o(\|h\|^2)\) along the stated regime.

notation.meaning: second subderivative of f at x-bar relative to v-bar

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order fidelity relative to a selected subgradient and a specified family of vanishing displacements.

source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I
Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The second-order model based at \((\bar x,\bar v)\) is faithful along a displacement regime \(H\ni h\to0\) when
\[f(\bar x+h)=f(\bar x)+\langle\bar v,h\rangle+\tfrac12 d^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(h)+r(h),\qquad \frac{r(h)}{\|h\|^2}\to0.\]
Directional fidelity restricts this limit to \(h=t w_t\) with \(t\downarrow0\) and \(w_t\to w\); uniform local fidelity requires the remainder estimate uniformly over normalized directions in the declared set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A second-order model is faithful when its prediction error is little-o of the squared step, either directionally or uniformly over the stated directions.
knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Model Fidelity

children.title: Active-Geometry Instability
children.top_down_role: Instability caused by changing active constraints, pieces, faces, or multiplier structures.

assumptions_latex: \(C=\mathbb{R}_+\) and \(N_C\) is the limiting normal-cone mapping.
The reference graph point is \((\bar x,\bar v)=(0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The active geometry is not locally constant, and \(DN_C(0\mid0)\) changes discontinuously with the direction.

notation.meaning: graphical derivative of the normal-cone mapping

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degenerate one-dimensional constraint illustrating loss of stable active-set identification.

source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis
Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At the degenerate graph point \((0,0)\), the graphical derivative of the normal cone to \(C=\mathbb{R}_+\) is
\[DN_C(0\mid0)(w)=\begin{cases}\{0\},&w>0,\\ \mathbb{R}_-,&w=0,\\ \varnothing,&w<0.\end{cases}\]
Thus arbitrarily small perturbations can select an interior regime, where the normal is fixed at zero, or a boundary regime with vertical normal variation. Any second-order formula presuming a locally fixed active geometry therefore fails without a nondegeneracy or identification condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a degenerate inequality boundary, infinitesimal directions select different active regimes, so normal-cone derivatives and active-set-based second-order models are unstable.
knowledge_statements.title: Active-Geometry Instability

children.title: Fast-Rate Degradation
children.top_down_role: Loss of favorable local convergence rates under inaccurate or unstable second-order information.

knowledge_statements.title: Fast-Rate Degradation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certification boundary for fast local rates under relative and absolute errors in an inexact second-order iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(e_k\to0\) and
\[e_{k+1}\le C\bigl(e_k^{1+\alpha}+\eta_k e_k+\delta_k\bigr),\qquad C>0,\quad 0<\alpha\le1,\]
with \(e_k,\eta_k,\delta_k\ge0\). If \(\eta_k=O(e_k^\alpha)\) and \(\delta_k=O(e_k^{1+\alpha})\), then this recursion yields \(e_{k+1}=O(e_k^{1+\alpha})\). If instead \(\eta_k\to\eta>0\) and \(\delta_k=0\), the recursion yields only a linear upper estimate. If \(\delta_k\not=o(e_k)\), it does not yield a superlinear estimate. These are certification boundaries of the displayed upper recursion, not necessary conditions on every iteration satisfying it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Errors that decay at the target fast-rate scale are sufficient for the recursion to certify that rate. Larger error terms weaken what the recursion can certify, but the upper bound alone does not prove necessary conditions or actual degradation.
assumptions_latex: For constants \(C>0\) and \(0<\alpha\le1\), the nonnegative quantities \(e_k,\eta_k,\delta_k\) satisfy \(e_{k+1}\le C(e_k^{1+\alpha}+\eta_k e_k+\delta_k)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conditions \(\eta_k=O(e_k^\alpha)\) and \(\delta_k=O(e_k^{1+\alpha})\) are sufficient for the recursion to certify order \(1+\alpha\); slower error decay weakens that certified estimate.

notation.meaning: distance of the kth iterate from the solution

children.title: Model–Rate Transfer Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on translating second-order model quality into local rate guarantees.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is locally Lipschitz, \(F(\bar x)=0\), and \(A_x\) is invertible with \(\sup_{x\to\bar x}\|A_x^{-1}\|<\infty\).
For \(0<\alpha\le1\), \(\|F(x+s)-F(x)-A_xs\|\le L\|s\|^{1+\alpha}\) locally.
The update is \(x^+=x-A_x^{-1}F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Locally, \(\|x^+-\bar x\|\le K\|x-\bar x\|^{1+\alpha}\) for some \(K>0\).

notation.meaning: local first-order model matrix at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional transfer from a uniformly invertible local model to a local convergence order.

source_refs.source_title: The Linear Complementarity Problem
Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\) sufficiently near \(\bar x\), set \(s=-A_x^{-1}F(x)\) and \(x^+=x+s\). Uniform inverse boundedness and local Lipschitz continuity give \(\|s\|=O(\|x-\bar x\|)\). The model estimate then transfers to
\[\|x^+-\bar x\|\le K\|x-\bar x\|^{1+\alpha}\]
for some \(K>0\). With only an \(o(\|s\|)\) model remainder one obtains a superlinear conclusion without a fixed power order; an \(O(\|s\|)\) remainder supports at most a linear estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform model invertibility transfers a remainder of order 1+α into convergence of order 1+α; weaker remainder control yields correspondingly weaker rates.
knowledge_statements.title: Model–Rate Transfer Boundaries

source_witnesses.source_title: The Linear Complementarity Problem

children.title: Local–Global Convergence Boundary
children.top_down_role: Separation between local second-order convergence theory and globalization mechanisms.

assumptions_latex: Newton's method is applied to a continuously differentiable scalar equation wherever the derivative is nonzero.
No line search, trust region, damping, or merit-function acceptance test is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local quadratic convergence near a simple root does not imply convergence from an arbitrary initial point.

notation.meaning: a simple real root of q

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical smooth example separating a valid local Newton theorem from global convergence.

source_refs.source_title: The Linear Complementarity Problem

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q(x)=x^3-2x+2\) and apply the undamped Newton map \(N(x)=x-q(x)/q'(x)\). Since \(N(0)=1\) and \(N(1)=0\), the initial point \(x_0=0\) generates a two-cycle and does not approach a root. Nevertheless, the negative real root \(\bar x\) is simple because \(q'(\bar x)\ne0\), so the standard local Newton theorem gives quadratic convergence for initial points sufficiently near \(\bar x\). Globalization requires additional acceptance or safeguarding mechanisms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For q(x)=x³−2x+2, undamped Newton cycles between 0 and 1 although it converges quadratically when started sufficiently near the simple negative root.
knowledge_statements.title: Local–Global Convergence Boundary

source_witnesses.source_title: The Linear Complementarity Problem

children.title: Exact-Representation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regularity regimes where second-order representations retain the required information.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is twice continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
\(\bar v=\nabla f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^2 f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w)=\langle w,\nabla^2f(\bar x)w\rangle\) and \(\partial^2f(\bar x,\bar v)(w)=\{\nabla^2f(\bar x)w\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reduction of variational second-order objects to the classical Hessian in the smooth regime.

source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I
Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Using the normalization
\[d^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w)=\liminf_{t\downarrow0,\,w'\to w}\frac{f(\bar x+t w')-f(\bar x)-t\langle\bar v,w'\rangle}{\tfrac12t^2},\]
one has the exact identities
\[d^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w)=\langle w,\nabla^2f(\bar x)w\rangle,\qquad \partial^2f(\bar x,\bar v)(w)=\{\nabla^2f(\bar x)w\}\]
for every \(w\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Thus both the scalar second-order expansion and the coderivative-based object are represented completely by the classical Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a C² function, the second subderivative is its Hessian quadratic form and the second-order subdifferential is the Hessian applied to the direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Representation Regimes

source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I
Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

children.title: Stable-Calculus Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes where second-order calculus remains exact or operationally stable.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-Calculus Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact second-subderivative calculus under a smooth additive perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every direction \(w\in\mathbb{R}^n\), smooth perturbation preserves twice epi-differentiability and yields the exact sum rule
\[d^2(f+g)(\bar x\mid\bar v+\nabla g(\bar x))(w)=d^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w)+\langle w,\nabla^2g(\bar x)w\rangle.\]
Thus the nonsmooth second-order term is stable under addition of \(g\), with the smooth contribution entering through its Hessian quadratic form; no additional second-order qualification is required for this smooth additive perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a twice continuously differentiable function preserves twice epi-differentiability and adds exactly its Hessian quadratic form to the second subderivative.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and twice epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x)\).
\(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is twice continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^2(f+g)(\bar x\mid\bar v+\nabla g(\bar x))(w)=d^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w)+\langle w,\nabla^2g(\bar x)w\rangle\) for every \(w\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
